fields.claim_quote: If any $A^{n-1}_{i,j}$ would be 0, that would mean that there would not be any path connecting those vertices. Thus, the graph would be disconnected.
fields.explanation: Mathlib checks that the original P3 is connected, its actual adjacency matrix is the displayed matrix A, and (A^2)_(0,1)=0. The entry counts walks of exactly two edges, while 0 and 1 are adjacent. In every bipartite graph the parity of a walk is fixed by its endpoint parts. Consequently the documented family of connected bipartite graphs with at least two vertices always has a zero in A^(n-1): for even n use a diagonal entry (odd walk length cannot return to its initial part), and for odd n use endpoints of any edge (even walk length cannot switch parts). The correct connectivity test uses (I+A)^(n-1), the source theorem itself, or the sum of powers from 0 through n-1: connected vertices have a simple path of length at most n-1 and the identity allows padding by stationary steps. The original P3 is a distinct-endpoint alternative to the original K2 diagonal example, so the failure is not confined to diagonal entries. The claim about A^(n-1) is an intermediate error; no sufficiency criterion based only on small diameter of a nonbipartite graph is asserted.
fields.flaw: The forward direction rests on the claim that if any entry A^{n-1}_{i,j} = 0 then there is no path connecting vertices i and j, hence the graph is disconnected (equivalently, that connectivity forces every entry of A^{n-1} to be nonzero). This is false: A^{n-1} counts walks of length exactly n-1, and a connected bipartite graph can have zero walks of that exact length between two connected vertices due to parity.
fields.source_context:
0001 | Let $G$ be graph on $n$ vertices, $A$ its adjacency matrix, and $I_{n}$ the $n\times n$ identity matrix. Prove that $G$ is connected iff the matrix $(I_{n} + A)^{n-1}$ has no 0s.
0002 | 
0003 | My proof:
0004 | 
0005 | *If the graph is connected the matrix $(I_{n} + A)^{n-1}$ has no 0s.*
0006 | 
0007 | The identity matrix  takes care of the non-zero values for the diagonal (otherwise the diagonals would be 0 since self-loops are disallowed in simple graphs).
0008 | If the graph is connected there must exist a path between any two vertices $u,v \in G$. $A^{n-1}_{i,j}$ represents the number of paths of length $n-1$ between any two vertices. If any $A^{n-1}_{i,j}$ would be 0, that would mean that there would not be any path connecting those vertices. Thus, the graph would be disconnected. But we assumed that it was connected
0009 | 
0010 | *If the matrix $(I_{n} + A)^{n-1}$ has no 0s then G is connected*
0011 | 
0012 | If every $(I_{n} + A)^{n-1}$ is non-zero this means that there exists at least one path of length $n - 1$ between any two vertices. If this is the case, the graph must be connected.
0013 | 
0014 | Is this correct?
fields.witness: Let G=P3 on {0,1,2}, with edges {0,1} and {1,2}. Its adjacency matrix is A=[[0,1,0],[1,0,1],[0,1,0]], and A²=[[1,0,1],[0,2,0],[1,0,1]]. Thus G is connected while (A²)01=0, although 0 and 1 are adjacent. Matrix powers count walks of exactly the indicated length. This refutes the intermediate inference about A^(n−1), not the stated criterion using (I+A)^(n−1).

scope_metadata.evidence_scope: The selected certificate proves connectedness of P3, agreement of the displayed matrix with its adjacency matrix, and (A²)01=0. It does not establish an enumeration count or execution of BFS or 2-coloring.
scope_metadata.source_kind: User proposed proof of a true connectivity criterion; challenged intermediate inference
scope_metadata.target_scope: The local inference from a zero entry of A^(n−1) to disconnectedness. The original criterion using (I+A)^(n−1) is not refuted.
